how: A member proposes the team mark and supplies possible locations that others offer to join.
Members call helpers to a located build and receive written commitments.
A brief commitment answers a located build proposal without requesting anything further.
Participants judge space scarce and starting a mark demanding too many accounts.
A proposed mark and location give volunteers something concrete around which to gather.
A located build proposal receives a bare written commitment.
Participants repeatedly explain how individual timed pixels become collective designs, including after the event.
Explaining timed individual placement makes collective drawing intelligible to newcomers without establishing that every explanation recruits a placer.
Participants propose a logo, supply a base image and consider converting a rival mark into an orca.
Participants seek a spot and report that the team mark is finished.
The help post precedes a direct reply reporting completion, without identifying which readers placed.
Coordinate links, a proposed scale, refresh instructions and pixel widths organize distributed painting.
A posted scale remains a proposal and cannot establish that a template settled design disagreement.
A participant recommends extra accounts for more offensive placements while another reports the cooldown.
Retrospective bot allegations and hand-built pride establish a legitimacy dispute rather than independently verified automation histories.
The visible extra-account recommendation serves an attack before sustained defense, so it does not demonstrate defense-driven automation.
An internal chat is created for expansion planning without evidence that its unseen deliberations established decisions or a coalition.
The stated purpose of the separate chat is coordinating enlargement rather than negotiating a multi-room alliance.
Self-assigned picture parts and shifts evidence limited task allocation, while mock management sanctions do not establish canvas command or test an across-room frequency.
Members offer overnight coverage, recall that offer and report watching and repairing changed pixels.
A completion report precedes the offered night shift that would keep the placed mark.
Participants warn of a reported plan for their location without demonstrating that the threatened takeover occurred.
Attribution addresses rival marks and competing retrospective claims rather than verified tracing of changes to the room's own mark.
Reported approval for expansion is followed by a neighbor's demand to stop at the approved border.
A neighbor claims authority over approved border space while participants dispute its permission and territorial claim.
A member reports informing the neighboring room of expansion plans, although the cross-room exchange itself is not available.
Expansion rather than demonstrated neighbor erosion supplies the explicit context for border negotiation.
Members ask expansion to spare nearby art and avoid interfering with other work.
Border talk supports restraint only among placers who recognize the neighbor's claim, while an expansionist expressly refuses it.
A cooperative member denies that one expansionist speaks for every member of the room.
The evidenced representative dispute disowns a dissenter rather than explicitly rejecting a negotiator's right to bind the room.
The border dispute elicits a claim of cooperative collective intent but does not establish authorized leadership or enforceable universal compliance.
A rival visitor reports repairing the team mark without citing an adopted exchange contract.
A request for outside assistance and retrospective visitor repair do not demonstrate that maintenance strain caused recruitment and delivered help.
A reciprocal-protection offer and border negotiation lack evidence of an ensuing completed help exchange.
Alliance proposals and warnings about other actors' alliances do not establish this room's coalition membership.
An expressed wish for an alliance does not establish a defense-driven transition into a coalition.
Suggested alternate locations do not establish relocation after loss of a completed team mark.
Scarcity before an established mark motivates attacking a rival rather than demonstrating movement after inability to hold a spot.
A participant explicitly answers scarce space and high account requirements by proposing concentrated destruction of a rival logo.
An attack call receives a reasoned objection to mocking others instead of organizing a mark.
The attack exchange receives an alternative proposal for adjacent logos and mutual protection without showing adoption.
A personal loss disclosure prompts apology within a hostile exchange without demonstrating whole-room reconciliation.
Participants explicitly describe the raid as stirring an existing hockey rivalry.
The same attack post names a disliked hockey franchise and specifies where to place the hostile blue dot.
Existing team jokes and praise language are reused in canvas taunts and outcome celebration.
Territorial warning becomes antisemitic joking, which must remain explicit rather than be recast as neutral national representation.
A member's overlapping identities elicit reassurance without a stated neutral position between the disputing rooms.
Members dispute whether hockey rivalry licenses jokes about economic suffering and deaths without reaching a common position.
A reply rejects retaliation through harmful jokes as inconsistent with how members should distinguish themselves from rivals.
A defense against economic mockery branches into substantive argument about the timetable and meaning of phasing out oil.
Mock management praise and sanctions license a parallel April Fools performance rather than canvas command.
Participants test whether praise differs from ordinary conduct and whether dated departure news is an April Fools claim.
Members criticize duplicate or deteriorating jokes while other participants extend the day's performance.
A fake moderator summons a familiar insult while separate replies enjoy players being pranked.
Members joke about moderators being dead and greet a moderator's return without addressing canvas organization.
A commenter announces removal of an aftermath guide as garbage, marking an intended content boundary.
An announced rejection of one post does not establish executed removal, moderator authority or a canvas-wide posting rule.
The visible intervention rejects an aftermath post's content rather than documenting a recruitment flood that prompted containment.
Participants celebrate finishing and surviving, turning the canvas outcome into a rare team victory.
The completion report itself announces shared accomplishment that later survival talk celebrates.
Members record the outcome, circulate media and review their own attempts in a timelapse.
Retrospective participants recount late entry through attacking before building, without proving that attack caused the later build.
Fatigue, admiration, relief at the ending and regret at missing participation coexist as different speakers' reflections.
Celebration and media sharing coexist in the outcome thread without demonstrating that pride caused preservation.
Regret about missing participation does not evidence a decision to preserve the effort in a future project.
Retrospective records and missed-participation regret provide no evidenced transition into a lasting project or emblem.
Post-event contention concerns script responsibility and the legitimacy of hand-building, not an evidenced shared-copy cleanup or a resolved account.
Members call for blue filling, propose converting a rival logo and report altering its shape.
The attack call explicitly substitutes for an unrealized build, as a later participant also recounts.
Members celebrate rivals' destroyed marks while taunts and defenses of the rivalry continue.
The named attack continues as rival-directed taunts and post-event victory claims.
An image-led guide is appreciated as a rivalry shitpost, but its unavailable visual content cannot be reconstructed independently from comments.
Reasoned pleas for restraint may be mocked rather than accepted, so individual objections do not establish collective cessation.
Perceived design complexity makes attacking a rival preferable to building for one participant, independently of the stated scarcity of territory.
A participant proposes threatening a rival's allied mark to frighten off its helpers, without evidence that the threat was carried out.
A visitor requests help holding another team's mark against a takeover, without a visible commitment to provide it.
